title: Job 34:1–15
context: Elihu continues his speech, now addressing the wise as well as Job. He summarizes Job’s complaints that God has taken away his right, and answers that God cannot do wickedness or pervert justice, and that all life depends on God’s breath. Readers evaluate Elihu differently: some see him preparing for the LORD’s speeches or correcting both Job and the friends, others see him repeating the friends’ errors or speaking presumptuously, and 42:7 does not name him. Both traditions hold God’s justice and creaturely dependence as shared ground, while debating whether Elihu applies them fairly to Job.

verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu speaks again, beginning a new section of his speech. The narrator simply introduces him.

Arminian readers, like others, weigh Elihu’s words carefully, since the book does not name him in the LORD’s verdict of 42:7.
verses.reformedNotes:
Interpreters differ on Elihu: some see him preparing for the LORD’s speeches or correcting both sides, others see him repeating the friends’ errors.

Reformed readers likewise hold these views variously. Both traditions read the verse as shared ground.

verses.text: “Hear my words, you wise men. Give ear to me, you who have knowledge.
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu calls on the wise and knowledgeable to hear his words. He addresses a wider audience.

Arminian readers note that Elihu appeals to the judgment of others, inviting them to weigh his argument rather than simply accept it.
verses.reformedNotes:
The ‘wise men’ may be the friends or listeners more generally; the text does not specify.

Reformed readers see Elihu presenting his case as one to be tested. Both traditions read this as shared ground and report his appeal without settling his standing.

verses.text: For the ear tries words, as the palate tastes food.
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu says the ear tests words as the palate tastes food. Discernment is required.

Arminian readers see a sound principle: words must be weighed, including Elihu’s own, before they are accepted as wise.
verses.reformedNotes:
The proverb also appears in Job’s own mouth (12:11), which suggests a shared wisdom tradition.

Reformed readers see the call to test all claims. Both traditions read this as shared ground about discernment, and note that readers are invited to test Elihu’s speech by the same standard.

verses.text: Let us choose for us that which is right. Let us know among ourselves what is good.
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu proposes that they choose together what is right and know among themselves what is good. He invites shared judgment.

Arminian readers see a reasonable invitation to deliberate, whatever one concludes about Elihu’s later application.
verses.reformedNotes:
Elihu presents himself as seeking justice rather than winning an argument, though readers differ on whether he succeeds.

Reformed readers see the value of seeking what is right together. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: For Job has said, ‘I am righteous, God has taken away my right.
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu reports Job as saying, ‘I am righteous, God has taken away my right.’ Elihu sums up Job’s complaint.

Arminian readers note that Job did speak of God taking away his right (27:2), so the summary has a basis.
verses.reformedNotes:
Job also said, “I hold fast to my righteousness” (27:6). Whether Elihu’s summary is fair to Job’s full meaning is debated.

Reformed readers likewise weigh the summary carefully. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: Notwithstanding my right I am considered a liar. My wound is incurable, though I am without disobedience.’
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu continues his summary: Job considers himself called a liar despite his right, with an incurable wound though without transgression. The picture is of protested innocence.

Arminian readers see a recognizable echo of Job’s laments.
verses.reformedNotes:
Elihu presents Job’s claims in compressed form. The prologue itself calls Job blameless (1:8), which complicates any simple judgment against him.

Reformed readers see Elihu framing Job’s words for rebuttal. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: What man is like Job, who drinks scorn like water,
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu asks what man is like Job, who drinks scorn like water. The image is harsh.

Arminian readers see Elihu accusing Job of treating mockery lightly, a charge the book does not clearly support.
verses.reformedNotes:
Whether Job is the one scorning or the one scorned is debated, but Elihu clearly intends a rebuke.

Reformed readers see sharp words that readers must weigh against the prologue. Both traditions read this as shared ground and report the charge as Elihu’s.

verses.text: who goes in company with the workers of iniquity, and walks with wicked men?
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu says Job keeps company with evildoers and walks with the wicked. The accusation is serious.

Arminian readers note that the narrative gives no evidence of such company, so the charge seems to rest on Elihu’s view of Job’s words.
verses.reformedNotes:
Elihu may mean that Job’s arguments place him alongside the wicked, rather than literal association, though the text is not explicit.

Reformed readers see a charge to be weighed, not adopted. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: For he has said, ‘It profits a man nothing that he should delight himself with God.’
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu reports Job as saying it profits a man nothing to delight himself with God. He cites a dangerous conclusion.

Arminian readers note that similar words appear in Job’s description of the wicked (21:15).
verses.reformedNotes:
Whether Job himself held this view, or Elihu attributes to him words Job placed in the mouths of the wicked, is debated.

Reformed readers see the question needing care. Both traditions read this as shared ground and do not settle whether the attribution is fair.

verses.text: “Therefore listen to me, you men of understanding: far be it from God, that he should do wickedness, from the Almighty, that he should commit iniquity.
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu declares, “far be it from God, that he should do wickedness, from the Almighty, that he should commit iniquity.” God’s justice is affirmed.

Arminian readers affirm this as true of God.
verses.reformedNotes:
The truth itself is shared ground between the traditions; whether Elihu applies it fairly to Job is debated.

Reformed readers equally affirm that God does no wrong. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground about God’s righteousness.

verses.text: For the work of a man he will give to him, and cause every man to find according to his ways.
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu says God repays a man according to his work and causes each to find according to his ways. Recompense is affirmed.

Arminian readers affirm that God judges justly and that human deeds matter before him.
verses.reformedNotes:
The principle is true in itself, but the book of Job resists reading every suffering as direct recompense, as the prologue shows.

Reformed readers affirm God’s just judgment. Both traditions read this as shared ground, while noting that Elihu’s use of it in Job’s case is debated.

verses.text: Yes surely, God will not do wickedly, neither will the Almighty pervert justice.
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu repeats that God will not act wickedly, nor will the Almighty pervert justice. The point is emphatic.

Arminian readers affirm the confession, which Job himself, in his own way, also assumes when he appeals to God.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse restates verse 10, underlining Elihu’s central claim.

Reformed readers affirm that God’s justice cannot be perverted. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground about God’s character, apart from how Elihu applies it.

verses.text: Who put him in charge of the earth? Or who has appointed him over the whole world?
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu asks who put God in charge of the earth or appointed him over the world. God’s authority is underived.

Arminian readers affirm that God rules by his own right, not by delegated power, as Creator of all.
verses.reformedNotes:
The question implies that the Creator answers to no higher authority.

Reformed readers see God’s sovereignty grounded in his own being. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s authority over creation and the absurdity of judging him by a higher standard.

verses.text: If he set his heart on himself, if he gathered to himself his spirit and his breath,
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu says that if God set his heart on himself and gathered his spirit and breath to himself, the consequences would follow. Life depends on God.

Arminian readers see every creature’s existence as sustained moment by moment by God.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse depends on verse 15 for its conclusion. Life is presented as God’s continuing gift.

Reformed readers see creaturely dependence on God’s sustaining power. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground about creaturely dependence.

verses.text: all flesh would perish together, and man would turn again to dust.
verses.arminianNotes:
All flesh would perish together, and man would return to dust. Mortality is total without God.

Arminian readers see human dependence on God plainly confessed, a truth both Job and Elihu affirm.
verses.reformedNotes:
The imagery of returning to dust recalls the creation account of humanity from the ground.

Reformed readers see God as the sustainer of all life. Both traditions read verses 14–15 as clear shared ground about creaturely dependence on God.
